stem: A binomial variable X has mean 4 and variance 2.4. Using these to recover its parameters, what is P(X is at least 1), to four decimals?

per_option_rationale.rationale: For a binomial, mean = np = 4 and variance = npq = 2.4. Divide: variance/mean = q = 2.4/4 = 0.6, so p = 0.4, and n = mean/p = 4/0.4 = 10. P(at least 1) = 1 - P(0) = 1 - q^n = 1 - 0.6^10 = 1 - 0.0060 = 0.9940.
Reports P(X = 0) = 0.6^10 = 0.0060, the complement of the event asked. Stopping at the zero-success probability answers the opposite question.
Uses 1 - p^n = 1 - 0.4^10 = 0.9999, putting the success probability p in the zero-success term. P(X = 0) carries q^n, not p^n, since zero successes means every trial failed.
Computes P(X = 1) = C(10,1)(0.4)(0.6)^9 = 0.0403, answering 'exactly one' rather than 'at least one'. At least one includes all of X = 1,2,...,10.

explanation: The parameters are hidden in the moments. Mean = np = 4 and variance = npq = 2.4. Dividing variance by mean cancels np and leaves q: q = 2.4/4 = 0.6, hence p = 0.4. Then n = mean/p = 4/0.4 = 10. 'At least one' is cheapest as the complement of zero: P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - q^n = 1 - 0.6^10 = 1 - 0.0060 = 0.9940.

explanation_sections.punchline: You are not handed p and n; recover them from the moments. variance/mean = q, then p = 1 - q and n = mean/p, and only then take 1 - q^n.
explanation_sections.approach: Model: binomial with unknown parameters. The decisive move is variance/mean = npq/np = q = 0.6, so p = 0.4 and n = 4/0.4 = 10. For at-least-one, use the complement of the zero term, which is q^n because zero successes requires every trial to fail. Subtract from 1.
explanation_sections.lesson: For a binomial, variance/mean = q. P(X = 0) = q^n always; the zero-success term carries q, never p.
explanation_sections.timing: About 165 seconds: one division for q, one for n, one power, one subtraction. Reject 0.0060 instantly, it is P(X = 0), the complement, not at-least-one.
